<reason>CON won by controlling the decisive frame: the motion mandates composting/hydrolysis specifically, not merely the end of permanent plots, and CON conceded the latter while forcing PRO to defend the former. PRO's defense eroded across rounds — "narrow accommodations" expanded by Rebuttal 2 into time-limited burial, ossuaries, niches, and private faith-cemetery transfers, which CON cleanly exposed as CON's own rotation program plus an escape hatch that resurrects the exact private-plot inequity PRO's opening condemned. PRO never answered that contradiction, never dislodged the Singapore/Hong Kong examples (which solve scarcity via tenure and columbaria without composting, and which CON turned against PRO's own showcase), and never closed the feasibility gap beyond assertion — "repealed in an afternoon" and "hundreds a year, then scale" against thousands of annual deaths and weeks-per-vessel throughput. PRO argued a coherent, dignified alternative vision and landed real rhetorical hits ("shovels and smokestacks," "place of return"), and its answers to pressure questions were honest, but its counter-claim that rotation merely "schedules" scarcity was asserted against a functioning real-world model. Both sides were epistemically disciplined and format-compliant; CON simply made the debate easier to decide, ending with the crystallized dilemma: a mandate PRO won't enforce is a slogan, and one it would enforce is coercion.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 1/Rebuttal 2 sequence on the accommodations trap: spotting that PRO's "narrow accommodations" either coerced grieving families or collapsed the mandate, then quoting PRO's own Rebuttal 2 menu (time-limited burial, ossuaries, niches, private faith cemeteries) as "my program plus an escape hatch" — with the private-cemetery option resurrecting the inequity PRO opened against. PRO never reconciled that contradiction, and it became the fulcrum of CON's closing.</best_rebuttal>
